speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to do so I would like to make reference on this, the last day of the session and probably of this Parliament, to the services rendered to Parliament and to freedom itself by you, Mr. Speaker, as the presiding off'cer during this and the previous Parliament.
Hear, Hear!

I do so as one who has served under several Speakers. What I am about to say represents, I think, the views of all members of the House who have been greatly impressed by the manner in which you have discharged your responsibilities.
I recall on one occasion a former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, saying in the House:
There are under British parliamentary institutions two symbols of authority-the Crown which speaks of the sovereignty of loyalty, the Speaker who speaks of the sovereignty of Parliament.
Much could be said, of you, Sir, all of which would be complimentary, but I can summarize what I have in mind by quoting from the translation of the Latin words on the throne that you occupy:
An impartial hand is an aroma
Mindful and faithful,
A mind conscious of rectitude.
You have discharged your duties with consummate ability. You have combined authority with compassion. The degree of impartiality you have displayed in the discharge of your duties has been such that you will always be looked back on by the present and future generations in this House as one who, in his person, epitomized the finest traditions of the Speakership.
I add one word respecting your wife who in the discharge of her duties has done so with a consideration and regard for the office you are holding and together you have honoured this institution.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might begin by saying that, as with many of the words of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, his words today are very thoughtful, very well said, very appropriate. But as often happens I cannot necessarily see myself agreeing with the premise, that is to say, that this is the
last day of this Parliament. I concede that I have less experience than the right hon. gentleman in such forecasting games, and therefore I am-
You lost last week.

As the hon. member says, I was not correct as to the date on which Parliament or this session might end. But because I have great confidence in the right hon. member's political acumen, I am at least prepared to concede the possibility of his premise-
Oh, oh!

-and therefore find it appropriate to say on behalf of all members of our caucus that we have had constant admiration and respect for your authority, Mr. Speaker.
ITranslation]
More particularly, although your talents as an orator are still unknown to most of us, your talents as Speaker are eminently visible. We have also been in a position, every day of this session, to see that we had good reason to respect your authority which was founded on a great deal of patience, much wisdom, an outstanding knowledge of parliamentary procedure and finally, on a sense of humour which always made us welcome your rulings even when they went against our wishes.

Mr. Speaker, I have not had the very long experience in Parliament that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has but I have had a little longer than the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), although not very much. May I put it to you this way, Sir, that in my several years in Parliament I have often come to the conclusion that the sign of the real greatness of a Speaker is when the only people who occasionally become annoyed with him are ministers of the Crown.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be gilding the lily and uncomfortable and embarrassing to you if I went on at length. I say to you, Sir, that every one of my colleagues has had the greatest admiration not only for the manner in which you have carried out your duties but for the fairness and impartiality which you have always shown, for the dignity you have exhibited throughout, a dignity that, to your great distress, you were not able to get from the members of the House on occasion.
I also join the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert in expressing my admiration of Madame Lamoureux and her companionship to you in your duties.

July 7, 1972
Tribute to Mr. Speaker
Some of us in my party at least, and I believe in other parties, had hoped that the admiration in which you have been held as Speaker would have persuaded everybody in the House to create a situation whereby you could continue as Speaker without having to fight elections on a partisan basis. I regret that this has not been done. I hope it may still be done, whether or not this is the last day of Parliament.
When we adjourn today, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that all of us will return to our constituencies with a feeling of admiration, respect and, what is perhaps more important, very deep affection for you as a person and as Speaker of this House.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Creditiste colleagues, I join the spokesmen of the other parties in expressing our admiration and thanking you for all that you have done for us in the past. I want to praise you not only for your fairness but also for your fine performance. May I thank you on behalf of the Canadian people, especially my constituents. I wholeheartedly agree with the kind words said about you and while voicing again our admiration, I wish you a long life and hope that you will again be with us at the next session.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps you would permit me, as your seatmate and as deputy leader of the independent group that sits in this corner of the House, to associate myself with the words that have been spoken by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the leaders of the other parties.
As a person who has had the pleasure of sitting in this House for many years I have come to respect and appreciate the wonderful contribution that you have made to this House and to the traditions that it embodies. It is not an easy task that you have filled so very well. It is a lonely position. Yet you have managed somehow to be kind but at the same time to be fair, to be gentle but at the same time to be just. This is a great tribute to you.
May I join in this expression of appreciation to you and to Madame Lamoureux who has stood by your side and who in her own right has made a very great contribution to the affairs of this country. May we wish you well, and health and happiness in the knowledge that you hold our respect and affection for the contribution you have made.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members will have noted that today I have not complained of the length of speeches.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Actually, I held back a little wondering whether there would be more contributors to the debate. If there are none, I will deliver a ruling. It will be a very simple one.
The words of praise that have just been spoken leave me speechless, which is obviously a very proper attitude

for the Speaker. I will, therefore, simply say from the bottom of my heart a very sincere thank you to hon. members. I want to assure them of my appreciation not only for the much too generous words that have just been spoken but also for the extraordinary co-operation they have extended to me during my term of office as Speaker of the House of Commons.
We all know, of course, that the Speaker cannot discharge his responsibilities in this House without the complete co-operation of hon. members, without their understanding, tolerance and charity. This has been given to me in large measure. For this I am extremely grateful to hon. members.

I thank you, dear colleagues, for your unfailing generosity to me and I wish you all good luck.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING CONTINUANCE OF FEDERAL FISCAL CONTRIBUTIONS UNDER MEDICAL CARE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement to the House with regard to the medical care program. Its purpose is simply to give notice, as required, under the statute.
Section 8 of the Medical Care Act obliges the government of Canada, at least six months before March 31, 1973, to review the amount and manner of payment of the federal fiscal contributions made under section 3 of the Act with a view to formulating proposals for any changes that may appear to be necessary or desirable with respect to the amount and manner of payment. This review has been conducted in the context of discussions with the provinces of the federal government's proposals in respect of health care financing.
I wish to state that the government does not propose any change at this time in the amount or manner of payment of the federal contributions referred to in section 3 of the Medical Care Act outside of the context of these discussions. The proposals under consideration, if implemented, would replace the existing formulae under both the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services and Medical Care Acts.

Mr. Speaker, as far as I
am aware we had no notice that the minister was going to make this statement. That being the case, there will be no comment at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has not given us very much information but what he has given us causes me a good deal of concern. What the minister is really saying is that he is notifying the provinces that, while there may be no changes at the present time, the government does intend to discontinue the present financial arrangement and negotiate some new arrangement.
Certainly the discussions that have been going on with the provinces indicate that the federal government intends to reduce the basis of its contributions. They also indicate that the federal government, instead of paying roughly 50 per cent of the cost, would prefer some new formula which would place a larger share of the cost of health insurance upon the provinces. While some provinces of Canada might be able to carry a larger share,

REQUEST FOR RETURN TO CUSTODY OF FOUR FEMALE MEMBERS OF SONS OF FREEDOM DOUKHOBORS- REASONS FOR RELEASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Solicitor General. What response has been made to the request of the Attorney General of British Columbia that four female members of the Sons of Freedom sect of the Doukhobors be returned to federal custody, and for what reasons were they released by the Commissioner of Penitentiaries?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RETURN TO CUSTODY OF FOUR FEMALE MEMBERS OF SONS OF FREEDOM DOUKHOBORS- REASONS FOR RELEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these people were granted temporary leave on medical grounds as three of them had been on a hunger strike since September 1970 and two others since August 1971. According to medical officers of the department and others who were consulted, their physical condition was very poor. It was a matter of life or death because they were fed forcibly through tubes.
We consulted the Department of Justice. Evidently, we had the right to force these people to eat, but not only in extreme cases where lives were jeopardized. On consulting Mr. Peterson, the Attorney General for British Columbia, we were told there was no objection although he did not want to be responsible for the final decision. We tried persuasion and we thought of commuting penalties, but we did not want to establish precedents. We consulted the Parole Board; they were not willing to grant leave. The only possibility left then, according to the law, was to grant temporary leave for medical reasons.
The decision was made public at the time and conveyed to the Attorney General of British Columbia who did not oppose it.
Four of those persons now face accusations before the courts. Another one is behaving very well indeed and Mr. Peterson has no objection to her continuing to enjoy her freedom. With regard to the other four, we are studying the possibilities open to us to ensure that they do not disturb society.

The House resumed, from Thursday, July 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Munro that Bill C-170, to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children, be read the third time and do pass, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) (p. 3655).

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night before ten o'clock I was appealing to all hon. members to realize that while the bill contains many errors and inequities its objective is to provide increases in benefits to the hundreds of thousands of poverty stricken children in this country. Surely, it is time that we got the message. I am tired of repeating it here so often. With all our rich resources, both material and human, there is still one-fifth of our population living in poverty and we do not seem to be able to cope with the problem. Surely we ought to have the common sense to realize that if we do not direct our efforts towards helping the children in the poverty stricken category, we will continue to have these same problems that we discuss almost daily in the House of Commons because these children with grow up to be poverty stricken adults. This will result from the government's failure to deal with its problem. Over the years many speakers have pointed out the government's inability to cope with the problems of the nation. Will someone stop and realize that it is the people of Canada, whether they be affluent, middle class or poor, who will judge the government's capabilities, and decide whether or not this bill is acceptable?
When are we going to realize the importance of our youth? When are we going to show a little bit of statesmanship by living up to the promises we make and fulfilling our responsibilities to the people we represent instead of continuing the political debate that goes on here? I have not heard anyone say anything about the children who will benefit under the provisions of this bill. I urge hon. members to think for a few moments about this. After listening to the debate it has become evident to me that some hon. members do not have poverty in their constituencies. Evidently many Members of Parliament do not visit the poorer sections of their areas, and see the shameful existence of too great a proportion of our citizens.
It is interesting to sit here and listen to those Members of Parliament who seem to have all the answers, those who know everything about everything, those who talk about what should be done and how it should be done. I listened carefully to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) give his advice on what should happen to make this country of ours a better place in which to live. He called the bill stupid, idiotic and incompetent. I agree that the bill has some terrible errors in it, but as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) said last night, there is still time to correct some of the errors. I remind the hon. member for Trinity that this bill, or various versions of it, has been hanging around since the
July 7, 1972

famous white paper on income security issued in 1970. Why did the hon. member for Trinity not speak up at that time rather than waiting until the report stage of the bill last Tuesday? He said that the bill filled his heart with despair. It fills my heart with despair when I get letters from constituents telling me they cannot afford to take their children to hospital, and that since they cannot pay school fees a school board will not allow their children in school.
The hon. member for Trinity called for guaranteed annual work instead of a guaranteed annual income. He and the leader of the NDP called for a reduction in the unemployment rate from 6 per cent to 3 per cent, and said if this were achieved there would be no need for welfare. I heartily agree with them, but how do we bring this about overnight? Surely, there are enough indications that the government has not been able to accomplish this objective. What are we going to do in the meantime? What are the thousands of poverty stricken children to do in the next number of years while waiting for the experts to provide a Shangri-la? The hon. member for Trinity also said that we should have a higher minimum wage-again I agree-and that our wealth should be distributed across the various regions. These are wise words and I agree with him, but I ask him when and how can we expect this to happen with this government? I ask him why this did not happen when he had some influence for some years in the cabinet? The member mentioned in his speech the other day the visits he made to garden parties, his talks on TV and interviews with many employees who said they would not work any extra overtime because they would lose all or most of it in taxes.
Well, I do not visit too many garden parties in my district, Mr. Speaker, and I do not appear on TV very often, but I can tell you I visit lots of homes in my district and I see first hand the conditions under which too many of our Canadian children are living. I talk to parents who wonder where the justice is, where all the employment is and where are all the hundreds of thousands of homes that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) tells us he is building for Canadians. I do not see any flurry of excitement in my district, Mr. Speaker, about building homes. Yes, Mr. Speaker, and while I am here in Ottawa I get hundreds of letters every week begging for help. These people do not have enough money to heat their homes, or money to buy food. I invite anyone here to come to my office and see these letters, Mr. Speaker. What am I to tell these people? Do I tell them to wait a few years more and we will reduce the rate of unemployment to 3 per cent, do I tell them to wait until we distribute our wealth in a more fair fashion? Do I tell them to wait until we find jobs for everyone?
I get very angry, too, when I hear that people on welfare do not want to work. I say that this is as irresponsible a comment as anyone can make. Again I say to anyone, come and look in my files and read with distress the number of letters I get from people who do not want to go on welfare and refuse to do so at great sacrifice.

No, Mr. Speaker, it is time we forgot about statistics and reports and studies on poverty, and remembered that we should start to think about our responsibility to give some humane consideration to this problem. We should be ashamed to have to admit that in this supposedly wealthy country of ours, one fifth of our population is living in poverty. This is a situation that must be corrected. There are too many children in this country in this category of our population who will continue to live in poverty, undernourished, living in hovels, with little or no medical care. Unless we provide for them, they will grow up in continued poverty, without proper development and education. This will mean that they will continue in poverty as adults, and it will be our fault in view of all the lessons we should have learned.
It has become obvious throughout the many committee meetings and debates, that the children of this country who need help will have to wait until next summer. The amendment introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) gives us the opportunity to show our concern and deal with some of the weaknesses of the bill at further committee meetings over the next couple of weeks without interfering with the ability of the minister's department to get the mechanics in motion and avoid further delays. Surely the minister would agree to this proposal, Mr. Speaker, and I say we should meet, even on Monday morning. At the same time, Mf. Speaker, the bill takes us part of the way towards reducing poverty and directing our efforts to the many people who will get benefits. In spite of the inequities in the bill, some of which will be a horrendous nightmare for the administrators as I pointed out last night, I hope we will vote for this bill because we are concerned for the poverty-stricken citizens of our country. The minister and the government evidently feel it is a good bill, but I am sure that many of their members do not agree.
If we, as Members of Parliament, and even the people of Canada who will not benefit from the bill, have any feelings within us to make a better Canadian nation, our efforts and our resources must be directed toward those who cannot provide for themselves. I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for pointing out that there is a military lesson which I learned many years ago which indicates that no army can advance any faster than its slowest or its weakest elements. With our richness in material and human resources, our country cannot grow and progress while one-fifth of our population remains hindered by its inability to keep up with our progress. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is our duty and it must be our duty as a state, to provide for the weak and to support the measure before us today.

The minister may claim that is oversimplified, but he is alleged to have made those remarks. Those remarks, even if oversimplified, are pertinent, since the Minister of National Health and Welfare is charged with the responsibility for social welfare programs, which include family allowances and medical care schemes, to which the provinces contribute in part.
Next, may I read what the Special Senate Committee on Poverty had to say on page 46 of its report entitled, "Poverty in Canada":
The popular notion that our tax system takes from the rich to give to the poor is a myth. Before the 1940s, during the Great Depression, there was some indication that an equalizing trend was taking place in the total amount of income shared before transfers. However, research done by the Royal Commission on Taxation (1966) demonstrates that, since the 1940s, our tax structure had surprisingly little effect on the profile of income distribution already described.
Governments rely on a regressive tax structure as a source of public revenue. (Regressive taxes are those which take away a higher proportion of income from the low-income groups than from the high-income groups.)
An examination of Table 18 shows that 56.5 per cent of the income of those earning less than $2,000 (before transfer payments) goes to paying taxes. If social-security contributions are included, this becomes 60 per cent of their income. By comparison, those with incomes over $10,000 pay only 37 to 38 per cent in taxes.
Let us remember that at one time individuals and corporations contributed about equal amounts in taxes. The trend in tax collection now is for corporations to contribute less than individuals. The corporate tax burden has been reduced by approximately 22 per cent, and the burden on the individual taxpayer correspondingly increased. With that in mind, I suggest the House ought to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) which, if accepted, would maintain the universality of this program.
May I point out that the minister, when making his speech in Quebec, was illogical in saying that the money for financing this program must come from the middle income group. After all, the government party and the official opposition are the captives of the corporate interests of this country and will carry out their policies. They will not introduce a tax system which will more justly raise revenue from all citizens of Canada, including those with corporate interests.
A professional person such as a school teacher with $10,000 per year in taxable income must pay $2,285 in taxes to the federal government. If somebody makes $10,000 in taxable income from a capital gain, that person will pay tax on only half that gain, the tax being $833. On the other hand, if a man receives $10,000 in taxable income from a Canadian registered corporation, he will pay on that $10,000 not $2,285, not $833, but a mere $193 or less. That is the kind of just society this government represents.

As the hon. member says, it will be worse. The middle income groups, those families earning $7,000, $11,000 or $12,000, will lose, for the most part, the family allowances that were introduced by a previous Liberal government and paid as a social right. At the same time, some in the middle income groups have been forced to contribute to unemployment insurance, even though the Unemployment Insurance Commission will do little for them. Such contributions are restrictive in that they decrease peoples' incomes.
Let us not fool ourselves by assuming that it will be easy to draw the line under the new family allowances program and say one family is justified in getting benefits and another is not. Consider, for instance, the situation of the farmer, and compare it with that of the teacher or the industrial worker. There is a time in people's lives, mostly when they are between 20 and 35, when they are trying to get established. Some people, even though they make $7,500, $8,000, or $8,500, at one time in their lives incur the expense of raising children. That is when they need family allowances. This program, which is to be based on selectivity, will reduce the incomes of those individuals. The family allowance under the old legislation was paid as a social right, and for many it is to be curtailed. Allow me to point out some of the figures involved.
A family, with one child, earning $4,500 a year will get $20 under this program. A family, with one child, earning $6,000 a year would get $15.05. If we assume in all cases that the family has one child, at $7,000 it will get $11.75; if it earns $8,000, it will get $8.45; if it earns $9,000, it will get $5.15; and when it reaches $10,000, in theory it will get $1.85 which is not payable.
Let us now consider a family with two children under 12 years old, since that is where the maximum benefit would be available. With an income of $5,000, it would receive $30; with $6,000, it would get $23.40; with $7,000, $16.80; with $8,000, $10.20; and with $9,000, $3.20. It must be remembered that for every increase of $100 in income the basic family allowance decreases by 33 cents. That is an added complication. Also, every time a child reaches 12 and enters the higher age bracket, the department must be notified. The amount of family allowance receivable will be changed. All this involves administrative work. When a child is born, the parents must inform the department and every time the family's fortunes change notification must be sent to the Department of National Health and Welfare. When income falls, the family must notify the department in the hope of obtaining a greater benefit; and when income increases, it must also notify the department. This is all very complicated. I do not know who was involved in the drawing up of this program.

By the time people reach the age at which they receive the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement, there is not the same fluctuation in their income as there is in that of young families between the ages of 20 and 35 or 40. The minister should not forget that.
In 1971, some of my constituents received so much a month for the basic old age pension plus the guaranteed income supplement. They received something like $115 or $117 a month. In April of this year, they found that $10 had been deducted. The same was done in May. No one told them the reason for this. They were not told that they were overpaid last year and that it was a mistake. It was not the fault of these people that they were overpaid, it was the fault of the administration. That is a minor problem in terms of the old age pension. It will be one of the major problems this legislation will create.
The unemployment rate in this country is 4.9 per cent. There are 512,000 people unemployed. We are aware of the job creating programs of this government. However, I do not see the need for developing a new bureaucracy in the Department of National Health and Welfare. Double the number of employees will be required to handle this inadequate and incomprehensible program. This program has been designed to bolster the poor of this country. The minister did not refer to any provision that would prevent the provincial governments making a readjustment under the Canada Assistance Plan so that if these payments increase, the poor people, those who rely on welfare, will have their payments reduced by the provincial governments under the Canada Assistance Plan. The minister should consider the fact that his name and his record as Minister of National Health and Welfare will be connected with this piece of legislation. I can assure the minister that I will be in his office quite often.
This country developed a social system, which is not by any means perfect, based on the concept of universality. It is based on the concept that family allowances are a social right. This allowance has been paid to the mothers of this country. In a sense, it represents an income and a respon-

sibility for them. To teach their children responsibility, the mothers often gave them the family allowance. In my family, the money was set aside for my university education. This was fundamental; it was very important and the money was very helpful.
With a program of selectivity, one million mothers in Canada will no longer receive family allowance payments. This is incomprehensible in the light of the manner in which the program was introduced. It is difficult to understand, considering the fact this government was elected in 1968 on the concept of a just society. Since this government has taken office, it has divided Canadians into the haves and have-nots. This government claimed it would hold this nation together. It has driven more wedges between the different sections and elements in this country than any government before it. This program, which is based on some kind of selectivity, could only be outlined by a technocrat sitting in an ivory tower deciding in a statistical manner how to deal with the people of Canada. Let us not forget that this government will be held responsible for this legislation.
It will be interesting to note how many thousands of dollars will be spent on publicizing this plan. A great deal of advertising was necessary this spring when the old age security plan was changed. In answer to a question which was placed on the order paper, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) was advised that hundreds of thousands of dollars had been spent on advertising and promoting that program. That will be a minor cost in comparison with what will be involved in trying to explain this program to the people of Canada. It will take a horde of Philadelphia or Toronto lawyers to figure this out. Even then, I am not sure they will be able to do it.
I would be interested in seeing the Minister of National Health and Welfare trying to explain and justify this piece of legislation to his constituents. After the very concrete criticisms and proposals which have been made by the New Democratic Party with regard to this legislation, I cannot conceive the logic or the reasoning of the minister in continuing with this program as it is now proposed. I hope he will see fit to support the amendment we have moved, a reasoned amendment based on universality and social right. The minister need not be concerned that should he accept this amendment we shall turn round and say: "We told you so". If he accepts the amendment I shall publicly praise him for his honesty and his strength. I want to tell the hon. member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Whelan) that if he will support our amendment I will do likewise. I believe this is a fundamental change in the restructuring of our social system. We are moving away from the concept that everyone has a right to receive such things as family allowances. We are dividing the people into the haves and the have-nots. We are putting labels on the haves and telling them they must bear the cost of bolstering the have-nots. I can remember having a meeting with union members in my area, a very strong element. They believed they should support any candidate who would endorse the programs in which they were interested, and even 15 years ago they were asking that family allowances be increased. I think I was able to get some of their support by agreeing that family allowances should be continued.
What really worries me is that the minister made a statement again today indicating that there would be a change in the amount the federal government is willing to put into some of the universal schemes which have been developed with the co-operation of the provinces. The government has also been making noises, not very coherent noises admittedly, about a guaranteed income which will get rid of much of the whole morass of government departments.
It was interesting to make a phone call yesterday to a provincial welfare administrator in my area asking him to intervene with a municipality over a temporary allowance to be given to a young fellow who unfortunately is in the Orillia School and has gone home. Unfortunately, he is over 21 and loses the advantage he had, which is provincial care while in that institution. While he is home for two months he cannot get a disability pension, although he is obviously disabled, because it takes six or eight weeks to get it from the provincial authorities so he will have to go to the municipality. That problem is duplicated in every office of every Member of Parliament almost every day.
There is a desire to get rid of this morass of detail, the slight difference between this program and how it interrelates with a fifth program, and so on. The government has been talking about doing something about this problem by the development of a guaranteed annual income. The Social Credit party said recently that it favoured the payment of an income to everyone in Canada based on a flat rate. I wish it were as simple as that. I should like to see an arrangement by which we could pay everybody a subsistence allowance. Then the tax structure would reclaim unneeded amounts. I suggest that if the government had thought about a guaranteed annual income, they would now be in a position that it could not be universal because I am sure there would be a needs test, a means test, an income test or a blood test which would be necessary before you could get that amount of money. That is what is wrong with the system.
We are really saying we cannot afford to give all the young people in Canada a reasonable amount of money for family allowance. This was to buy shoes, extra books and a little extra for the children themselves. The mother was to administer it and she was to have it. We are saying this is not possible now, we cannot do it for everybody. We can only do it for one class of the people. This is not good
July 7, 1972

enough. The rich are not going to agree with it. The poor are not going to agree with it and the middle class are not going to be willing to finance it.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the House took recess.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was urging, and continue to urge, the minister and members of the House to give consideration to the amendment in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) which, very simply, would provide the increase for all those in receipt of family allowances and would not eliminate a large portion of the people in this country who we believe are entitled to this increase. I think a government which does not consider increasing either pensions or benefits for any other segment of the social field is, in effect, downgrading its interest and participation in family allowances. It may be that the government wishes to get rid of the family allowance structure. If so, the government should say so. It has been interesting that in this debate not even some of the Conservatives went so far as to say we should get rid of this type of payment to children.
It has been argued very forcibly both here and elsewhere that this type of legislation leads to an increase in the population. In keeping with modern ideas, perhaps for those interested in population control there is some repugnance in the idea of family allowances which are really a recognition of an added financial responsibility for those people who have children. The government, however, has not really reached this conclusion. Of course, I believe it would be wrong to agree to any consideration of such a prospect.
It is interesting to look at the payments which have been made under family allowances. When we originally started these payments back in 1944, there was very great disparity between various areas and regions in Canada in terms of population expansion. The population expansion in the east was considerably greater than it was in other parts of Canada. One of the charges made in those days was that these allowances in respect of large-sized families had an effect on the population increase. I believe it is safe to say that, particularly in the province of Quebec, the birth rate was phenomenally high. It was phenomenally high for two reasons. I believe there was a religious reason and a rural reason, both of which tended to increase the population.
The fact that in 1944 many families in the province of Quebec received very large sums of money was considered by some to be an indication that this type of assistance was wrong and, therefore, should be discontinued. In looking over the situation in the years since 1944, it is
Family Income Security Plan
interesting to see that circumstances have changed. Although family allowances are still being paid, and while they are really a production bonus, this has really not affected the birth rate in that province. The birth rate in Quebec has been reduced to equal that of any region in Canada and is, in fact, one of the lowest birth rates in the civilized world. The argument that this type of production bonus has created an undesirable situation-and I say "undesirable" from the point of view of the environmentalist who looks at the global situation in terms of overproduction of homo sapiens-is not necessarily a good argument in respect of whether or not we should produce our own citizens or bring them in from somewhere else. I believe I would favour the home-grown population increase rather than an increase through immigration from abroad.
The fact is that the money we pay in respect of family allowances has not encouraged an increase in population. It has not done anything to advance the number of people who have been born. I think everyone, particularly those interested in the social side of the picture, will agree that family allowances in the main when introduced represented a considerable asset with regard to family development in many parts of the country. It meant mainly two things. First of all it established for the mother and the housewife an amount of money that she would have in her own right to distribute to her children as she observed their specific needs. It was not designated for clothing, milk or food, but was designated for the mother to distribute to her children in the best manner for the benefit of the family. I think it is safe to say that the amount paid in 1944 did bring about some change because personally I know of families which were able to buy books for their children so that they would be able to attend school. They were able to buy the necessities and clothing so that the children could attend school. It enabled these children to participate with other children with a degree of equity that they would not have been able to enjoy had it not been for this sum of money.
I think most members will agree that initially that was the use to which this money was put. It is a discredit to successive governments since 1944 that they have not meaningfully escalated the family allowance payment to bring it up to a level that would at least meet the present rise in the cost of living. Such an escalator clause has not been put in the bill. Other speakers have used figures and made comparisons to show that the cost of living has gone up two and a half times, therefore the family allowance should have gone up by the same amount. Since it did not, it has meant that a poor family has had far less spending power, and poor families are not all in the low income group. A poor family may be living in mortgage row in a very expensive house, have a very expensive car, and the mother and father may have expensive tastes, yet you may find in that family a desperate need for some of the essentials that is probably equal to that of a family in the low income group. It does seem to me that equality should be retained, and the government has not done that. It is my opinion that we would be much fairer in our treatment of young people if we were to retain the principle of universality which they have enjoyed over the years and which has enabled these young people to provide their families with the necessities.

July 7, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
It seems to me that family allowances should be provided to all at the maximum or minimum level proposed by the minister in this bill. I suggest that our standard of living and our productivity would indicate that the minister is not being generous at all; in fact, he is being niggardly in raising the amounts only to those levels proposed in the bill. Obviously, if the cost of living has gone up, if the gross national product has gone up and revenues have gone up, we should be able to supply as much money to children today in terms of today's dollar as we were able to provide to children in 1944 when this act was introduced. We are not doing that, we are reneging on one million mothers in Canada by creating selectivity in this bill, a principle which was not originally contemplated.
In terms of the social impact of this legislation, was it true that in 1944, very close to the end of the war, we did not have any poor, we did not have any rich and there were no people in between? In what category were these people, in what economic strata were they that we found it necessary to adopt universality in providing this type of care to all mothers on behalf of their children? What has changed? The minister says that he disagrees with the slogan which has been credited to him, probably erroneously, but it is a nice one. It is that you save the rich, soak the middle class and seduce the poor. Perhaps there is some truth in it. Perhaps we have a new class of people who like paying taxes, a new class of people who like receiving money and a new class of people who do not like to pay their share. If that is so, then my guess is that it has always been so; there has not been any change or any reduction in the need. Those who originally believed in 1944 that it was not fair in social terms to divide children into economic categories should be heard, because in my opinion they still constitute the majority in Canada and they are probably the most numerous group of people even in this Parliament.
I am sure that most of the Liberal members will be going to their ridings very shortly and will be awaiting the call for a federal election. Are they really going to tell the people in their constituencies that we have had to give up social equality in the family allowance structure so that we can pay the poor, that we are only interested in helping the welfare cases in this country? Will some of those Liberals not be saying that they believe that all children in Canada should have the benefit of family allowances because they are Canadians? I think there are many members in the House who will not be selling the government's policy, and I am sure they will have great difficulty in explaining the two or three other recent programs in which selectivity is incorporated. I may not be smart enough, and I am sure my party is not smart enough-in fact I am not sure if anybody is-to follow the reasoning of the government behind this change, but I am sure that the average person in Canada would like to get rid of all the divisive factors in our society and would like to provide equality wherever possible. I am sure we would not want to see a woman having to make the decision as to whether or not she should do a limited amount of work because that may mean her children will receive less assistance in family allowance if she does so. I am sure that the average Canadian wants equality.

I have heard very little argument in this country from any political source or from any of the social agencies against the idea of a universal guaranteed income. One of the reasons people are interested in adopting the universal guaranteed income is that it will apply to all people, it will do away with computerization in solving social problems and it will do away with the necessity of having inspectors coming into people's homes. This legislation will mean that decisions will be made by computers and inspectors will have to check these decisions. The average individual will have to make declarations of various kinds every time his income or his family situation is altered in any way. This will be applied to the information which will come from the Department of National Revenue. Officials in charge of this program will have to check the information regarding family allowances against the National Revenue figures. An inspector will come from both of these departments and will harass that family with things that they really do not understand. I am sure that the country does not want that.
The present government seems to think we are so bankrupt that we are unable to provide for Canadians, that we have to divide the rich from the poor, the haves from the have-nots. I am sure that Canadians would not want that. They will not agree with it, particularly since we went through a futile exercise a couple of weeks ago in one minor field of government expenditures. We found that almost $700,000 was being wasted on providing information which was really self-glorification of the government and its agencies. We suggested that it could be eliminated. Mr. Speaker, you will recall that there were a number of votes and the sitting went on until a late hour, but the exercise was futile in the first place.
There is not a member who cannot stand up and say, "I know where we could save $1 million or $1 billion." A couple of weeks ago we were talking about information supplied by departments and by Information Canada. At that time we were talking about something like $1 billion, a billion dollars to sell the Department of National Health and Welfare, a billion dollars to sell the Department of National Defence, a billion dollars to sell all the government departments. Why not put that money into a social program? If the minister were to say, "Let us get rid of family allowances and the guaranteed income supplement; let us get rid of some of these schemes and substitute one plan that would apply to all Canadians," it is possible that I would be in favour of it. But I am afraid that here we are talking about doing away with universality in our social service structure, and substituting a class structure.
At present, old people who are poor have to make application for additional assistance. Originally, old age assistance was given to everyone who reached a certain age. Now, a certain amount of pension is given to everyone on reaching that age, but it is just about half of what it costs to maintain body and soul, and a means test is applied to those who seek an additional amount. Now, we are doing with the universal family allowance. I strongly urge reconsideration of the idea of selectivity, of dividing people up into classes. I firmly believe that almost all mothers in Canada use whatever money they get for the
July 7, 1972

benefit of their children. I know it is said that many family allowance cheques are cashed in the beer parlour, or corner grocery store, but I believe the benefit of the money is applied to the children. No matter how poor people are, they try to take care of their children.
Aside from the argument of selectivity versus universality, I believe we have an obligation to provide for escalation of payments according to increases in the cost of living. Even bodies as heartless as the Canadian Pacific Railway and the directors of the Canadian National Railway have now applied an escalation factor to their workers' pensions. This is true even of as heartless an agency as the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario. But it is not done with respect to family allowances. It is calculated that a 1944 dollar will purchase only the equivalent of 40 cents in 1972. If that is so, a family allowance payment of $16 per child per month is needed in terms of our present standard of living.
I suggest to those Members of Parliament who will be going home shortly that they whould give serious consideration to supporting the amendment, which would provide every child in Canada with the benefit of escalation of allowances in relation to the cost of living and the increase in the cost of living over the last 18 years. If Liberal members cannot do this in good conscience, then it is an admission on their part that they fail, through their amended income tax structure, to get money back from those who do not need it. They know that if they give the baby bonus to the rich, the rich are not taxed at the same levels as others, and will get more benefit out of that bonus.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the speech delivered today by the hon. member for Humber-St. Georges-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). I have complete sympathy with respect to the problems of his constituents. I am just as concerned about the children of his constituency and of this country as is anyone else, but I still believe that this is a stupid law, and we will be sorry if we let it pass this afternoon. Frankly, I cannot understand why it was introduced in its present form in the first place. In my opinion, it represents the most inappropriate and, in the long run, ineffective solution to what is for many people in this country a very serious problem.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe asked why I did not speak sooner. I should like to point out to him that I have been speaking about the fundamentals involved for a long time. I have spoken both outside and inside the House about the alternatives and how they could be achieved. I have been talking about the positive alternatives which are more effective and more humane. I have been shouting it from the hilltops. I have been saying that there is a better way but few people have been listening. I wrote a book to explain, on the basis of the knowledge I have gained over many years in public and private life, how we got into this mess and how we might go about getting out of it. Not too many people have taken the trouble to read what I had to say.
Mr. Speaker, we have to make fundamental changes if we want to solve some of the problems I have been talking about. This persistence with band-aid treatment will
Family Income Security Plan
never do the job. By putting one band-aid on top of another all we do is exacerbate an already difficult situation. If we want to tackle the real problems in this country we have to do it by fundamental means. These fundamental means are jobs and wages. In the long run, there is no other way to achieve the goals that we want and that is the point of view I should like to discuss. We would have to introduce a system whereby for employables there would be ample opportunities to work for decent wages and, of course, for those who are unable to work due to enforced idleness or because they are incapable, an income sufficient for their requirements.
The amendment before the House offers an opportunity for reconsideration. I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) with great interest and she made a most impressive speech, one that was worth listening to and worth reading. She spoke eloquently of the needs of the poor people in this country and she spoke compassionately as she always does. I would like to see this House take seriously some of the things she said.
In so far as options are concerned, there are several, of course. The first option would be to refer this bill back to committee and to reconsider the advisability of the universal approach. The payments could be increased under that system of universality which was established in 1944. That would solve the problems, at least in the short run, which were raised by my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe. Then, of course, if that were the solution we could use the present income tax laws, perhaps with some changes that would be appropriate, to make sure that the benefits of the increase went largely to those who need it, the people at the bottom end of the income scale. That is what the tax laws are for; that is the reason we have a graduated income tax which is very steep in its application. It is, in fact, a redistribution of income. There is no reason in the world why this same technique could not be used if we wished to stay with the universal approach.
The advantages of staying with the universal approach are that it is easy to administer-perhaps I should not say it is easy to administer but compared to this new bill it is easy to administer. The comparison would be the comparison between night and day. It does my heart good to hear the New Democratic Party complain about the increasing bureaucracy in this country. I think this is one of the most desirable and beneficial developments that I have noticed in a long time. Everyone is beginning to recognize that we must have a simpler solution. We cannot go on forever complicating things to the point where we have more and more people passing paper, more and more people on the payroll, fewer and fewer people producing the wealth whilst all of us spend more and more time answering questions, filling out forms and standing in line because of some regulation which may not apply adequately in some cases.
A symptom of this was expressed during the question period today when someone mentioned the experience of a small businessman who was fined $100 for not filling out one of those silly forms sent out by Statistics Canada. I have great sympathy with the small businessman. The bureaucrats of this country are driving him crazy and worse than that they are driving him out of business. In a

July 7, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
few years there will not be any small businessmen because they will not be able to survive. Ultimately, they are going to say "A pox on it, we will go to work for the government and go home at three minutes to four every day". What a sad reflection that would be on the traditions which we hold dear. I am not just thinking of traditions, Mr. Speaker, because tradition is only important if it has a continuing function, but of the relationship between businessmen and their customers which really only comes with small organizations and which will be nothing but a distant memory if we proceed much further in the direction we are going. As a result of having operated a small business, I know that now the entrepreneur spends most of his time filling out forms. I have talked to a number of small shopkeepers and businessmen this year, and I know that they take home less pay than any one who works for them. Who would expect them to survive for long under these circumstances? The principle applies to all of us and it is applying more and more to the very people we are trying to help.
What kind of form will we have to fill out in connection with this law? The minister has told us that it will not be any more complicated than the income tax form. I do not know whether other hon. members had the same reaction to that interjection as I, but I thought to myself that he just cannot be serious. The minister is making a case for his own bill and he says that the form will not be any more complicated than the income tax form so we do not need to worry about it. The thing that drives us crazy once a year now will be done four or five times a year by the poor. Perhaps they will learn to enjoy it because they will not have time to do anything else. Mr. Speaker, we can get used to anything. Certainly, the universal system would be less complicated than the one the government proposes. I must admit that I agree with my New Democratic Party friends that it would be socially more acceptable. I know the NDP do not like me to agree with them, and I shall try not to do it too often but I must admit that sometimes they say things with which I can agree.
Mr. Speaker, I do not like to see the country divided the way this bill will divide it. I think the bill is regressive, and I think it just introduces one more division in the country based upon social and economic standing in the community. I think it would be much more acceptable socially if we were to stay away from the introduction of one more means test, particularly one as complicated and hopeless in its application in ordinary circumstances as this one is destined to be.
The second option would be not to increase the levels of family allowances but to leave them at their present rates and try another approach to providing the extra purchasing power needed by the people in this country who are below the poverty line. I admit, frankly, that I prefer the second approach. There need not be poverty in Canada, and the fact that there is more poverty in Canada today, relatively, than there was a few years ago when the antipoverty campaign was begun is a reflection on the ineffectiveness of the band aid treatments which have been instituted.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we need a little more enterprise; that would be the solution. I should like the hon. member to give due and just consideration to what I will say about this. In my opinion, there is no reason in the world, except bad management, for the 6 per cent unemployment rate in this country today.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
This is not happening in other countries. I know the government can point with some comfort, I suppose that is the right word, to the experience in the United States, an experience which is about as bad as ours. The reason, I suspect, is that many of the theologians in charge of the United States economy were trained in the same schools and read the same bibles as the theologians who have been in charge of our economy. There is no excuse for this unemployment, none whatsoever. Most countries of the western world do not have unemployment at these levels. Only in Canada, the United States, Italy and Great Britain is a level anything like ours accepted.
I should like to outline three steps that ought to be taken if we are to have full employment. The first step consists of a further reduction in taxes at the low income levels. The last budget may have been successful in offsetting the effects of the American DISC program. It may have provided a stimulus for industry, but it did nothing on the other side of the economic equasion-it did nothing to increase aggregate demand. One could ask why business would want to expand considerably if, at the same time, there is not sufficient purchasing power in the hands of people who need goods and services. Why would business expand if there is not that capability in the hands of the people for purchasing the products of business, if there is not that capability in their hands which, in the first instance, would induce business to provide extra goods and services? So, if we want to get our economy back on the road, if we want to get it rolling again, we must provide an infusion of purchasing power. The best way of infusing that purchasing power is by providing tax relief for those people who need food, shelter and clothing, who need the necessities of life about which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe talked. Lower taxes would provide an immediate infusion of money into the economy and create the demand which would create jobs which, in turn, would stimulate the economy and get the economy rolling again.
The second step, of course, because, mathematically steps one and two are related, is increasing the total amount of effective demand which would set the total level of employment. Economists call total effective demand total aggregate demand. That is the regulator which sets the total employment level in the country, and anyone who has even a faint knowledge of the dismal science of economics is familiar with that. So, if we want to provide sufficient economic demand to create meaningful employment for the people of this country who want to work, we must increase total aggregate demand. This means, in effect, that we must increase the money supply, as the government has been doing, or rather as the central
July 7, 1972

bank has been doing, to the point that interest rates are driven down.
How can people who want to buy a house afford a house if they must pay 9 per cent interest on the mortgage? That is beyond the reach of the average person in this country. There is no way that the average citizen can buy a home for which he must pay over a period of 35 or 40 years if the mortgage interest rate is 9 per cent. Further, how can the people of this country begin small businesses, corner grocery stores and similar small businesses of any kind, if on the money they borrow they must pay 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent or 14 per cent interest? There is no way they can do that, Mr. Speaker. There is no way that people who want to do something for themselves, who want to become involved in the economic system, can branch out in business if the economic dice are loaded against them as heavily as they are at present. So, the second step must be increasing the money supply and driving interest rates down.
The third step is one that the people in authority in this country have rejected. The people who have responsibility for the management of the economy of the country have resisted the No. 3 step which must be taken, the imposition of mandatory wage and price guidelines in this country, the only effective way to control monopoly power.

There is no alternative, Mr. Speaker, to this step in view of what has happened in the last few years. The lack of effective controls and mandatory guidelines has distorted the entire economy, pulled it out of shape, to
Family Income Security Plan
the point where, today, in all ten provinces a married man with two children can get more on welfare than he can by taking a job at minimum or near minimum wage rates. In many cases people can get more by drawing unemployment insurance than by working. I say to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe that this is true in his province as well. I was told recently of a manufacturer in that province who owns three factories. He cannot fill them with workmen, even though there is a high rate of unemployment on the island. I am not saying this is bad; but I am saying that this shows that, often, people across this country can make more by not working than by working.
The inevitable result, of course, is disaster from all points of view for this country. First, on the economic side, with more people drawing welfare or unemployment insurance, more people are taking from the national income produced and there are fewer working. Consequently, the total pie is smaller than it otherwise would have been and there is less for everyone. Second, we must remember the social distortions that result from people not working. They become used to doing nothing and find it more and more difficult eventually to re-enter the labour force.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
If there were a Liberal party in this country it would be fighting monopoly power, fighting General Motors for building front ends that either smash in or fall out, fighting doctors for leaving patients unattended, fighting strikers for not picking up garbage, and fighting the vested interests on behalf of the people of this country. That is what a Liberal party would be doing.
The fact that there is no Liberal party in this country causes much pain and distress to some of us. The government is so involved in band-aid treatments that for one reason or another it has managed to avoid looking at the principles. The principles are Liberal principles. If they would go back to them they would know what to do. The Liberal principle is that when the rights and freedoms of any individual or group in society reaches the point where they trample on the rights or freedoms of another individual or group, they have to be curtailed. The government has not effectively done this in so far as labour and management are concerned. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) can laugh, but he is as guilty as anyone in this government.
The philosophy of Liberalism is in ill hands at the present time. This government is totally removed from and unaware of what Liberalism means. They continue to allow wages and prices to get out of pace with productivity; they do nothing about it. Three years ago the government said it was going to control inflation even if it meant creating 6 per cent unemployment. That is precisely what it did. Now, 300,000 families in this country are in misery economically because this government put them there.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
That is how they got there. That is the truth. The tight money policy of 1969-70 is the cause of the present level of unemployment. That is one reason the government is now going to such extraordinary lengths to do something about it. If they do not do something about it, it is because they are unaware of the facts. I was interested to learn this morning that new opportunities programs will be introduced. Some of them may be worth while but in many cases it will just be another opportunity for the favourite few of the government to spend a lot of someone else's money; for the majority the only opportunity will be to pay higher taxes.
There is another alternative and I would like hon. members to think about it. We do not have to stay with this outworn, outmoded trade-off theory which the professional economists are pawning off on us. This is nonsense, but it will persist in the minds of the experts as long as you have monopoly power on both the labour and the industrial side pushing up wages and prices out of step with productivity. As long as that continues, the central bank has no recourse except to be involved in this trade-off between too much unemployment and too much inflation

or, as we have at the present time, too much of both simultaneously.
We should go back to fundamentals. That is the reason I intend to support the amendment. The committee would do well to take a hard look at this bill and what was proposed last night by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). She referred to this incredible bureaucracy as a Saint Vitus's dance; I thought it was a most eloquent phrase. Why do we persist in solutions which are so complicated and insensitive to humanity that they get everyone in this country uptight as a result? Surely there is a better way. If the committee cannot come up with one, I will be surprised. As a matter of fact, if given a free choice I will be surprised if the minister does not do that. We should refer the bill back to committee.
The frustration that one feels in a situation like this is real and understandable. Here is a bill that very few people like. Someone told me last night that a group of young programmers, people who learn to put information into computers at school, was largely responsible. I do not know who is responsible for it, but whoever it is I hope he has to live with it and has something docked from his pay every time the computer throws out false information. It is a horrendous prospect.
Members of Parliament, including many Liberal backbenchers and the people of this country realize that this is a poor bill. Many Liberal backbenchers do not want to fight the next election with this bill hanging over their heads. I know this from talking to them. They think it is more bureaucratic nonsense that the system did not have a chance to throw over. Opposition members are divided: some want to get ahead with it, not because they think it is the right solution but failing another solution they feel that half a loaf is better than none. Some want to get on with the job, taking the chance that they will be able to unravel the whole ball of yarn later.
The New Democratic Party made it clear that they do not like the bill. They say it is a bureaucratic monstrosity which removes the principle of universality that has worked satisfactorily over the years. I would venture to guess that given a free vote on conscience the vote of this House would be negative on the bill; it would not carry. I would go so far as to say that the same thing could happen in the country. The people of this country have more sense; they would be able to come up with a better solution. They would not do anything as complicated as this. They would reject this further intrusion into their lives and privacy. They would say that there has to be a better means of distributing income. They want opportunities and meaningful wages. The people of this country want the government to make it possible to start small businesses and do the things they want to do. They want the government to get off their backs with its tight money policy, regulations, bureaucracy and all the other things we have had that make life so complicated and take all the joy out of it.
I understand, but I do not like to understand, that when so many people are against the bill, when the prevailing opinion is negative and so many people think it can be improved or, better still, that it should be scrapped and started over again, nevertheless the bill will be passed because of the old party system of cracking the whip. The
July 7, 1972

whip cracks down and everyone jumps into line whether they agree or not. When the vote is called and the leader stands up, everyone falls into line even though their conscience says no.
Is it any wonder that the young people of this country are cynical about politics? Is it any wonder that the people generally have become cynical about politics? Is it any wonder that when you talk to them they say, "These ideas make sense, but will anybody listen?" Are you not just beating your head against a wall?" Is it not a sad state of affairs that the Canadian people should be losing faith in democracy because once a government has been elected they have no control over it and it persists in doing things of which the people would not approve if they had an opportunity to vote in a referendum. They say, "What difference does it make who we vote for, because the same thing goes on and on." The whip cracks, the bell is rung and the bill goes through; that is the situation.
I personally regret that one after another four or five bills have gone through which do not really make sense for Canada. Some of them can perhaps be reversed. But it is just like the Viet Nam war; you get into it inch by inch and there is no way of getting out. You get all the bureaucracy built in. So much face would be lost if things were changed. The time to avoid that trap is before you cross all the thresholds, before you get too far down the road.
I hope someone else will speak this afternoon. I hope the amendment carries and that the bill is referred back to committee, because if we as representatives of the people cannot come up with something better than this bill on behalf of those who need help, we should be ashamed.

consideration given to controversial or bills other subjects in committee. Some contend that committees are successful in the United States. Under the American system they are, because it does not matter in a committee what decision is made in either the House of Representatives or Congress; it does not directly affect the presidency of the United States or the leadership of the party in the presidential office.
However, it is different here. I do not care which political party is in office, because when a measure of a controversial nature is submitted to a committee, members vote on the basis of their political persuasion because to do otherwise, were they supporters of the government, would be to weaken the government.
The hon. member for Trinity said that this Parliament had ceased to hold the respect of the Canadian people. I agree. I find everywhere across the nation the view expressed that the institution of Parliament in these days is no longer effective. If that be so, then we might as well close down the institution. However, it need not be so for much longer for the Canadian people have an opportunity to make a change and to once more bring about the restoration of this institution. While we may differ in our views sitting, as we do, either to your right or your left, Mr. Speaker, there should none the less not be any requirement on members of the House to park their consciences at the door of Parliament. As I view it, that is the great danger today.
With regard to the present motion, I know that there are members in the House who in their hearts entirely support the need for further consideration being given this matter in committee. But they cannot vote that way because to do so would weaken their government.
Where are we going today? I recall when in 1944 the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King introduced family allowance legislation in this House. My own party was opposed to it and I was alone in caucus on the issue for several days. I said I was determined to support it and it was pointed out to me that if I did so it would be contrary to the viewpoint of my own party. Yet I stood my ground. A Member of Parliament is not an automaton to be pushed around as a puppet. Finally my party joined in support of family allowances in this House, with one exception.
With regard to old age pensions, this party has given its support through the years. During my period of administration we raised the amounts of pensions very considerably. We thought that the $6 increase given by the St. Laurent government in 1957 was unjust and unfair and we made sure in the next election that the "six buck boys" did not ride again. I am in favour of fair social security measures. But what do we face here, Mr. Speaker? We face a government that refuses to accept the principle of universality. Today we have the highest taxation in Canada's history. I should like to put on the record what the minister said in the immortal speech that he made in Quebec City. I said "immortal", but as far as the Canadian taxpayer is concerned it was an immoral speech and aimed against the middle class of this country. At page 18 of his speech he said:
Governments, contrary to what many may think, are not uniformly indifferent or hostile, impersonal or heartless institutions.
I have never heard anyone say that they were, but we now have the imprimatur of the minister.
They are composed of people who genuinely seek the aristotelian mean-
That indicates a knowledge of the classics.
-the maximum good that can be evenly distributed.
Aristotle never thought of that, but today he is blamed in the minister's speech. The minister then goes on to say:
To take the example which most concerns us here to day, measures to alleviate poverty-to increase the economic and social security of those now living a marginal existence-result only from transfers of resources which, in one way or another, come from those who are better off.
That is where the members of this House come in. Unfortunately, we do not have enough of the "super-rich" to effect this transfer only from the manifestly affluent. Resource transfers of any magnitude must come from the great middle class-those who provide the overwhelming majority of the tax revenue, but do not by any means see themselves as having reached Easy Street- or fat city, to use the term of the poverty ghettos.
What does that mean? In the next paragraph the minister said:
We cannot act like Leacock's horseman and go madly galloping off in all directions at once.
He should have given that advice to his fellow ministers because that is what they have been doing in this session in advance of an election. If this government is returned, then in view of what the minister said in Quebec City the middle class of Canada should know what is going to

happen to them. Today they are taxed as never before. But they have only just seen the sunrise; taxes are going to go up even further. Let me read what the minister said in this connection when speaking in Hamilton on June 28:
We must convince the middle-income groups that they are the only source of income adequate enough for taxation to really aid low-income groups.
As the hon. member for Trinity said, people are taxed today until in many cases there is no incentive left. In anticipation of an election the prospect is that we have not seen the half of it yet. The government has in mind increasing taxation for the middle class. This is the first time in recorded history that a government has gone to the people and has said that, so far as the middle class is concerned, if they think they have paid through the nose up to the present time, they have not seen the half of what they will be subjected to. The minister went on to say:
If you tax the top groups more, you would run into the law of diminishing returns-
Surely the law of diminishing return applies to those people whose incomes are between $8,000 and $15,000. But not according to the minister.
-because there are not many in that group and you would kill their incentive.
It would ruin the incentive of the high income groups to pay any additional tax, so they have already received some relief in the recent budget. The minister went on to say:
The same would apply to a 10 per cent increase in corporation tax, which would produce only $250 million in revenue-
Hence the tax collectors cannot touch the corporations and they cannot touch the rich. When in that position, what do they do? They will soak the middle class. That is what the minister's speech means. He goes on to say that if we had a 10 per cent increase in corporation tax this could harm incentive among companies facing stiff increases. There you have the picture. The top boys will not pay. They already had a slash on their income tax. Those on the bottom cannot pay.
