subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT POLICY OF CBC REGARDING CORPORATION-PRODUCED PROGRAMS BE REFERRED TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of preventing or delaying the showing in Windsor of corporation-produced television series or programs in order to sell these series or programs more profitably to broadcasting networks in the United States be referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts for investigation and report.
C.B.C. Broadcasting Policy
He said: The background of this motion, Mr. Speaker, is that three times within the last year-and-a-half the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has denied to television station CKLW, channel 9, in Windsor the right to carry Canadian-produced television series being carried over the rest of the CBC network. The first two series, "Audubon Theatre" and "Adventures in Rainbow Country", where the CBC was the co-producer with independent producer Ralph Ellis of Manitou Productions in Toronto, were denied to CKLW-TV during the 1970-71 season. The withholding of the third series, "The Whiteoaks of Jalna", where the CBC was the sole producer, occurred in January of this year.
In the first two cases the series were erroneously released to CKLW-TV and withdrawn only after the CBC discovered its error. In fact, 22 of the 26 instalments of "Rainbow Country" were shown in Windsor before the series was withdrawn. With respect to "Jalna" the CBC intended a delay of nine months in the Windsor release after the January 23 premiere on the rest of the CBC network. However, when it was not able to sell "Jalna" to the American networks even with the sacrifice of the Windsor market, it allowed the series to begin in Windsor on June 18, a delay of five months rather than nine.
After the two instances of CBC discrimination against Windsor last year I raised the subject in the House on April 5, 1971, at the time of adjournment, and in reply the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State read a statement prepared by the CBC. In that statement the CBC claimed that it released all full network programs to all stations of the English television network, including affiliated stations such as CKLW-TV in Windsor, with three stated exceptions.
The exceptions were as follows: first, with respect to television series produced in the United States and acquired by the CBC from a Canadian distributor for full English television network release, in which case the rights acquired by the Canadian distributor seldom include Windsor, since American distributors regard Windsor as part of the Detroit market; second, with respect to television series produced in Canada by independent producers and acquired by the CBC from a Canadian distributor for full English television release, in which case the CBC usually defers for a period of some months the right to include Windsor in its network schedule in order to increase the private producer's chances for United States sales; third, with respect to television series produced in Canada which are cofinanced or co-produced by the CBC, in which case the CBC again usually defers its Windsor rights to assist the private production company with its cost-recovery problems. It is readily apparent that the "Jalna" series, which was produced entirely by the CBC with taxpayers' money, does not fall under any of these exceptions, and therefore by the CBC's own statement ought to have been released to CKLW-TV.
To amplify the problems which CKLW-TV has with border-protection clauses, I should like to underline that the station is denied about 25 hours a week of American programming which is available to all other stations in the CBC network. Included are such popular programs as Flip Wilson, The Carol Burnett Show, Laugh-In, The Par-

July 7, 1972
C.B.C. Broadcasting Policy
tridge Family, The Jimmy Stewart Show, Walt Disney productions and specials like those of Jacques Cousteau. In these cases the decision to deny the Windsor television station access to the programs is made by the American networks, in the interest of having Windsor viewers watch the programs on the network stations in Detroit.
An allied border-protection problem is the denial to Windsor sports fans of the opportunity of seeing hockey games played by Canadian teams which conflict with home engagements of the Detroit Red Wings, or baseball games played by the Montreal Expos which conflict with those of the Detroit Tigers. In such cases the programs are not available to viewers anywhere in the Windsor-Detroit area. Again the decision is made by American interests, and it might be assumed that the CBC is here in the position of an unwilling accomplice.
Even though American network programs denied to channel 9 remain available to Windsor viewers, there is still a serious consequence. Since CKLW-TV does not have first-run American network programs as lead-ins for Canadian programs, it is able to attract a much smaller proportion of the audience to Canadian productions than it would otherwise be able to do. As a result, channel 9 has only 23 per cent of the Windsor audience and only 7 per cent of the Detroit audience. It is worth remarking that the station is able to attract a higher 12 per cent of the Detroit market for its American programs even though these are limited to re-runs of earlier American network programs. Its best lead-in, however, is its 9 p.m. local news program. With respect to its competitive position vis-a-vis American stations in Detroit, CKLW-TV is further affected by the fact that CRTC regulations do not allow it to carry many of the advertisements that can be broadcast in the United States.
The financial situation of the station is of public relevance because it affects the quality of programming which it can afford and also because of the CBC's purchase of a 25 per cent interest in the station in 1970 and its contract to take over 100 per cent ownership on May 31, 1975. The Auditor General's report recently revealed that CKLW-TV lost $3,135,000 in its first 13 months of operation and that the CBC will eventually be responsible for all losses sustained by its present principal owners, Baton Broadcasting Ltd. of Toronto.
The bleak financial picture is somewhat alleviated by the fact that $838,000 of this initial loss was for depreciation in the value of feature films which Baton Broadcasting had had to purchase, along with the station, from the previous owners, RKO General, at Detroit market prices which are much higher than those for Windsor alone. The introduction of Canadian content quotas will prevent CKLW-TV from showing many of the films before its rights run out.
It is also worth remarking that CKLW-TV has been adjudged to have made such an imaginative contribution toward local programming that it has recently won the Canadian Association of Broadcasters' award as the Television Station of the Year for 1972. Its 9 p.m. local news program and its efforts to promote the United Community Service campaign have been especially outstand-

ing. It should be added that it makes no effort to do any local programming for Detroit. However, it remains true that the 40 per cent of the schedule which consists of U.S. re-runs has to finance the 60 per cent of the schedule which is Canadian. Channel 9 has a constant struggle to avoid being a re-run and old movie station.
The CBC has recently been subjected to criticism for entering into an allegedly one-sided deal in favour of Baton Broadcasting and its chief shareholder, Mr. John Bassett. However, this was not an ordinary market transaction but, rather, one into which the CBC was forced by the CRTC, which required it to assume an immediate equity position and to guarantee total acquisition in the near future. In return for the financing of the acquisition of the station by Baton Broadcasting and its turning it over to the CBC at the acquisition price at the end of a five-year period, the CBC agreed to reimburse Baton for its interest and carrying charges and for its share of any operating losses during the period.
This appears to be a reasonable enough arrangement for the CBC to enter into. At the same time, the station will tend to be a financial liability for the CBC when it takes it over in 1975. Indeed, since its advertising policy is more stringent than that of the CRTC, its financial position may well be worse than that of the present management.
Many of the financial disadvantages of CKLW-TV are inescapable regardless of who operates the station, but the CBC's own border-protection policy is not. It is this which adds the final indignity to the situation. Dr. George Davidson, president of CBC, was quoted by Ron Base in the Windsor Star of January 17, 1972, as saying in an interview: "The thing I'm concerned about is the position of the Windsor station when it becomes CBC-owned and operated. I'm saying frankly that when that happens it will have to be treated like any other CBC station." To a Windsorite these words are not so much a reassuring conclusion about what will happen in mid-1975 as a discouraging reiteration of the CBC's intention to maintain the status quo as long as it can. The CBC expresses, not repentance but confirmation in sin.
The peculiar reasoning behind the CBC's border-protection policy is highlighted by the attitude it displayed in April of this year regarding the televising of the quarterfinal games in the National Hockey League play-offs. Since the Detroit Red Wings did not gain the play-offs, there was no border-protection clause to interfere with channel 9's carrying the games. If the NABET strike had not been in progress at the CBC at the time, channel 9 could merely have joined the CBC network. However, as a result of the strike McLaren Advertising, which handles the television rights of the games for the NHL, transferred those rights to the CTV network from the CBC.
As a station whose licence from the CRTC provides that it should carry CTV programs, CKLW-TV applied to the CBC under its affiliation agreement for permission to carry this CTV program. The CBC refused permission on the ground that this would involve splitting the network. This argument struck television viewers in Windsor as a mere rationalization, in light of the CBC's willingness to split the network to the disadvantage of Windsor viewers
July 7, 1972

whenever there appeared to be a possibility of financial advantage to it in so doing.
The hockey deadlock was broken by a combination of two factors: CKLW-TV carried the CBC network program as it was required to do, but paid WTVS, channel 56, a non-network UHF station in Detroit, to carry the first quarter-final games for it on April 5 and 6. This pressure, coupled with probable pressure on the CBC from the CRTC, induced the CBC to change its policy on April 7, and from the third game onward CKLW-TV was allowed to join the CTV network to present the rest of the playoffs to Windsor sports fans.
In its statement of April 5, 1971, the CBC ranks the economic factor of increasing the private producer's chances for U.S. sales-and, presumably, its own chances where it is the sole producer, though, of course, it does not admit the possibility of border protection in such a case- over any cultural factors, or indeed over any economic factor relating to the well-being of channel 9. But in point of fact it has not succeeded in selling in the United States any of the programs denied Windsor, so that the economic benefit which it places above all else is not actual but is at best potential.
On the other hand, it has been shown that no actual financial detriment occurs by allowing channel 9 viewers to see programs in advance of or at the same time as the rest of the Detroit market. The BBC sold its series on "Henry VIII" to a major U.S. network even though it had been previously shown on channel 9. Even more striking is the fact that "Harvey", an American special shown on March 22 of this year, was seen on channel 9 at the same time as on U.S. stations. This resulted from the fact that "Harvey" was taped at John Bassett's production studios at CFTO-TV in Toronto and was also shown on the CTV network. Mr. Bassett successfully insisted that any show produced at his studios and shown on the CTV network must be made available to Windsor.
The only conclusion possible is that the CBC's giving in to border-protection pressures, real, potential or imaginary, is an indication of commercial ineptitude. In actuality, no benefit has accrued to the CBC from border protection. In actuality, no detriment has occurred to other networks which have refused to discriminate against Windsor. In actuality, there is no economic sense to the CBC's economic argument. I need hardly add that there is no non-economic argument to which the CBC could appeal, since its position is, from the socio-cultural viewpoint, an absurdity.
In sum, the CBC policy with respect to Windsor television is a tissue of contradictions. A CBC-produced television series was denied to Windsor viewers on January 23, 1972, in contravention of the CBC's own announced policy of April 5, 1971. Channel 9 is beggared by the CBC even though it will have to pick up in 1975 the deficit to which its own policies contribute. The CBC denies programs to Windsor to gain selling advantages in the United States and then fails to sell in that market.
The president of the CBC recognizes that the CBC will have to abandon as untenable in 1975 policies which it now insists on following. The network can easily be split to Windsor's detriment when it is deemed to be advantageous to the CBC, but when a program split would be
C.B.C. Broadcasting Policy
advantageous to Windsor it is found to be inconsistent and illogical. The CBC, which exists to promote Canadian culture, attempts to limit its availability in Windsor. Of such insubstantial stuff is the CBC's policy towards Windsor fabricated.
In conclusion, I would ask the House to support my motion to refer this CBC mistreatment of Windsor to the broadcasting committee for a thorough investigation, one which would allow the intensive questioning of top CBC officials. I am convinced that such a study and the eventual report of the committee would bring about a change in the present unenlightened and discriminatory policy of the corporation.
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that "Jalna" is the CBC's "Ed-sel", as president-designate Picard has remarked, but residents of the automotive city of Windsor have the expertise and judgment to carry out their own vehicle tests. It is this cultural choice, so vital to a healthy democratic society, which they are being denied by the CBC. I hope that the CBC will be able, like the rest of us, to accept the consequences of democracy.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT POLICY OF CBC REGARDING CORPORATION-PRODUCED PROGRAMS BE REFERRED TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that in what may be the last debate of the twenty-eighth Parliament we should be dealing with one of the aspects of national identity. There was a debate of short duration a couple of days ago arising out of the Dominion Day episode. That had to do with our identity. This debate, however, brings us into the equally important arena in which we ask, "How are we to hold on to things Canadian and maintain Canadian values when our large neighbour to the south threatens to overwhelm us?"
From the point of view of the economics of this situation, I would imagine that the Windsor area stands alone. If one examines all the other cultural confrontations along the American-Canadian border one realizes for instance, that Montreal is vast enough to overwhelm any influence of Palm Springs, Maine and similar areas on the other side of the border. Toronto, perhaps, has a much tougher time dealing with the influence of Buffalo; but it is a city large enough to cope adequately with the situation.
Windsor, smaller than Detroit, really is in the nutcracker in this problem. Western Canadian cities are large enough to hold off American challenges. That is the nature of this kind of economics. One area of Canada, represented by, among others, the hon. member who has just spoken, has been suffering because of the desire of some Canadians at least to make dents in the American television market.
If we examine the statistics regarding viewer preference of television stations, the Americans, being much more parochial than Canadians and much more nationalistic-minded, probably will not be seduced over to a Canadian station in any event. They tend to follow the mass media and basic television fare. Our noble experiments in Canada will attract but few.
As for "Jalna," perhaps it is a mercy that the residents of Windsor did not have to see it when the rest of us did. It gives the knowing Windsor person an opportunity to write

to someone on the outside to find out what the series was all about. Maybe they could have the program translated into simple terms. It was an extraordinarily difficult production to follow. I enjoyed it, but I did not understand it.
This was a strange year in dealing with estimates of the government. One of the largest and most controversial agencies, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, did not have its representatives appear before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. This was partly due to the protracted labour difficulties that had gone on between the CBC and NABET. The fact is that when the deadline arrived by which the estimates were to be considered, those of the CBC were not subjected to scrutiny and, perforce, they were passed pursuant to the Standing Order of the House of Commons. It might have been there that the hon. member could have made his mark earlier this session. I realize that he is asking for this matter to be referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. I will support his motion in that regard, but it is a hollow thing. I do not imagine the members of that committee would be overjoyed with the prospect of trooping back to hold hearings this summer. In any event, the hon. member has not indicated that is what he wants to do.
I am sorry the hon. member did not take up this matter when the season of original shows was in full bloom, rather than the present season of re-runs. We could then have called witnesses. It would have given us a chance to examine the CBC on its philosophy without getting mixed up with their labour situation. Perhaps the most ironic factor in this whole strange business involving the Windsor television station is that the CBC, in the interest of expediency and trying to make some sales to the United States, found it necessary to turn its back on the mandate Parliament had given to it. The CBC was formed four decades ago to help Canada achieve its identity, stay together as a nation and help foster Canadians as actors, broadcasters, writers, musicians and all the fields of the dramatic arts. I think it would be this point which would most exercise us if we were to examine the Windsor problem in the broadcasting committee this summer. If not, it will certainly exercise the members of the broadcasting committee who will deal with it at the next session or in the new Parliament.
The CBC has always been tripped when it has shown itself to be overwhelmed by the cashbox mentality. In any event, it has not been conspicuously successful in that regard. It has certainly become a very bad cropper on this Windsor issue. It has left the people of that area down and has not shown a Canadian spirit by adopting the policy that it has adopted. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I will support the hon. member's motion.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT POLICY OF CBC REGARDING CORPORATION-PRODUCED PROGRAMS BE REFERRED TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) about the problems of the television station in Windsor, which is next door to the metropolis of Detroit. As the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) said, the general purport and philosophy of this motion will find favour with all members of the House. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville is aware of the problems surrounding private members' motions. In general, mem-

bers usually support each other's private motions and discuss them at length, so they rarely come to a vote. Even if this motion came to a vote, in view of the fact we are in the closing minutes of this session, and perhaps in the closing minutes of this twenty-eight Parliament, it is difficult to see what could be done in a meaningful way.
I listened carefully to the explanation of the motion. When I heard some of the scuttlebutt I thought the hon. member was moving a motion to have the House try to bring "Jalna" to the Windsor residents. I have great regard for the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville. He was a very esteemed chairman of the constitutional committee which travelled from coast to coast dissecting or trying to arrive at a new charter for Canada. He came in contact with many Canadians. I am relieved to find that, being exposed to Canadians from coast to coast, he was not taking the time of the House to try to have "Jalna" brought to the people of Windsor, good people though they may be. As the hon. member said, "Jalna" has become an "Edsel." I watched it once or twice and I really started to wonder about the CBC.
I think another hon. member wants to contribute his thoughts in respect of another area of discrimination in television service. However, I would like to make a few points. I agree with the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants that it is rather ironic that in the closing hours of this session, or this Parliament we are talking about communications. Communications is one of the real problems in trying to define something that is called Canada. There was worry about the physical bindings which hold this country together, whether they are the CPR, the CNR or the Intercolonial Railway. It was the physical approach that helped to bind this nation. Now we have electronic highways, electronic air. But communications is one of the cohesives or adhesives of a nation.
In Atlantic Canada, where I come from, you turn on the news in western Nova Scotia and invariably get the cookie sale in the Moncton baptist church, or you turn on the news from CBC or CTV in western Nova Scotia and you find out what the Saint John Girl Guides have done at their Brownie festival.
The CBC should not only help to correct the problem of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville but should start to correct the discrimination existing in other areas of Canada, particularly in Atlantic Canada where all we get in Nova Scotia is news from New Brunswick-their news, their stories, their cookie fairs, New Brunswick teas. We are in Nova Scotia and we want Nova Scotia news. It is one thing to have an airport called Halifax, which sometimes gets fogged in, and to have to land in Moncton-I have nothing against Moncton or the province-but I would like to know what Quebec would do if the alternate airport serving a Quebec airport were in Ontario.
I think it is an insult to the jurisdiction of Nova Scotia that the alternative to the Nova Scotia airport should be in another province, four hours away from Halifax. But in transportation we have to accept the fact that sometimes there is fog in Halifax and we have to land in Moncton even though Greenwood, one of the best air bases in western Nova Scotia, is available and is free from fog.
July 7, 1972

The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), both former ministers of national defence, know the attributes of Greenwood and know there is no fog there. I am glad to be the member from this area which has no fog, even though sometimes I may try to create a little. Be that as it may, there is discrimination on the part of the CBC.
There are only a few minutes left, Mr. Speaker, and there are many other serious things I wish to say. However the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville has brought to the floor of this House in the closing moments of this Parliament a question with respect to the CBC which I think every Canadian taxpayer wishes to see raised before the relevant committee of the House.
We did not take the opportunity this year to discuss the CBC estimates, because of the NABET strike. We did not want to get involved in that sensitive jurisdictional conflict. But the budget this year amounted, I think, to some $190 million. The fact is that the CBC during my time in the House over the last five years has more than doubled its operating budget. This makes the expenses for running the CNR a picnic by comparison. It is time we looked at the operations of this corporation. Maybe one of the good things emerging from the NABET strike is that Canadians managed without a CBC service and were able to live without it and enjoy the programs they received from alternative networks or through cablevision.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville mentioned the CRTC. There are a whole raft of problems connected with the CRTC, cable vision, Canadian content and the whole issue of communications. I, too, hope this whole list of items will be referred to the new broadcasting committee if there is a dissolution of this House before we next meet, or, should the House reconvene in September, that we will deal with it then.
As far as the NABET strike is concerned, it took us years in Atlantic Canada to get the national news at eleven o'clock, the same as every other Canadian community. For some incomprehensible reason, even though the strike is settled, we are still getting the national news at twelve o'clock. This may be thought to be a small and picayune point, but I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, if you watch the national news, that you imagine watching it around twelve o'clock until 12.30 or 12.45. Since we are such God-fearing folk in the east who go to bed early and like to get up early to work a hard day, that difference of an hour at night has quite an adverse effect on our physiology, let alone our psychology. So in these two ways we are affected.
I completely agree with the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville. I was a member of the broadcasting committee and I know he was involved, indeed, overinvolved, in the constitutional issue. I referred to him in jest as the Marco-Polo of the constitution, the way he moved all across the country trying to resolve that large problem. Today, in the dying minutes of this session he is trying to resolve a more local problem. He has my deep sympathy. But I do not want it to stay there: the CBC must expedite its plans for satellite service in western Nova Scotia. It is not good enough to say we will get satellite coverage in Nova Scotia in five years to give us reception in Nova Scotia from Nova Scotia rather than getting it from Maine or New Brunswick.

As far as the national news is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I do not see why, if the staff is in Toronto and the equipment is there-and it was not damaged during the strike- a couple of people not sitting on their buttons could fail to send the national news at eleven o'clock right across this land. So the hon. member has my sympathy and I hope we do something about this problem in the new session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the motion before us. I appreciate the motive of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) in the dying moment of this session and in the immediate pre-election period when something of this nature might be useful by way of improving his local fame.
Although I am prepared to consider his cry for some small thing of the nature of an alternative program, it does not seem very important to me. After all, I have to take into consideration the fact that almost 90 per cent of the geographical area of my constituency is not serviced by any kind of television service. Here we have a situation where the hon. member's constituents are exposed to a great variety of television stations and programs of all kinds, yet he is crying about them not being able to see "Jalna." Those of us who did see some of it, particularly myself, had a great desire to put a motion before the House to take the program off CBC television-and I am not trying to be critical of the efforts which were made by those who produced the show. I realize that those efforts were intended in part to effect an increase in Canadian content, but I think we all agree it was rather an amateur effort and in my opinion the viewers of Windsor-Walkerville did not miss much.
I should like to deal briefly with the absence of a television service in northern Alberta. Consider towns like Fort Vermilion, High Level and Fort Chippewyan, each having a population of 1,500 to 2,000 or more, where there is absolutely no exposure to direct television viewing at all. One of the biggest complaints I receive when I visit these areas is that my constituents do not have the opportunity tq see their Member of Parliament on television. That is a various serious matter, I think hon. members will agree.

speechtext:
It is a very serious matter. People should be able to get the direct news and views from Parliament, to which they are entitled. The citizens of Windsor-Walkerville certainly have not suffered that kind of serious deprivation. Over the four years in which I have been here I think it is fair to say that the CBC has been involved in several controversies, whether over programming, lack of service to certain areas or labour relations. In any event, they seemed to be involved in greater difficulties than one would expect for a Crown corporation.
I have given this matter a great deal of thought and have several suggestions to make which I think would improve the efficiency of this corporation. I do not want to be misinterpreted: I do not want it to be thought that the people working in the CBC as reporters, those in the press gallery and in this area, are not doing a very fine job. Most of them are sincerely trying to do a fine job. But if you look at the corporation as a whole it is not very

difficult to agree that there is a degree of efficiency lacking in the corporation. For example, if we look at the coverage given by the CBC of a convention or meeting and the coverage given by a private station, it would appear that almost always the CBC has at least double the staff of the private corporation.
I do not know whether that is the result of union demands, an effort to do a better job or is sheer inefficiency. But in view of the fact that it is a public corporation that is responsible to the public an operation that is paid for in large part out of the public purse, we should look at ways of making the operation a little more efficient. I think experience in the past in other areas have shown that some participation by private enterprise almost always has the effect of improving the efficiency of an operation of this kind or the operation of any kind of business.
Therefore, I suggest that consideration be given to the sale of part of the CBC to private enterprise, perhaps on a 50-50 basis or on some other basis, thus incorporating into the administration of the CBC that element of efficiency [DOT] which comes from private enterprise, which has to pay its own way. That suggestion is prompted in part by the fact that during the past four years I have been making efforts to get services into northern areas but have been told not to get too excited, that a satellite is just about to be fired into the sky and that everyone will receive TV service and be happy.
I cannot blame the CBC for the absence of such a satellite today. I can only blame the laziness of the government, as portrayed by a good number of its ministers involved in the satellite program. Four years ago I was told that a satellite would be up in two years. We are told today, four years later, that it will take another two years.
It is a little discouraging to my people back home constantly to write them year after year and say that we expect a satellite to be up in two years, that receiving stations will then be built and they will have the pleasure of receiving the same privilege as is enjoyed by the rest of the country and seeing direct television on a live basis.
I have received communications from some of the educators in the area, for example the principal of a school who did a study of student marks on current events and their knowledge of current activities in this country. It was his impression that those students who were not exposed to direct news and public affairs programs, or to television viewing, were less informed on various topics. Therefore, from the education point of view his conclusions were that it is definitely detrimental to students attending school in such areas to be denied such facilities. I would be inclined to agree that is probably true. There is no question that education is not the only matter of importance which is a benefit from viewing television; television is also recreational. Unfortunately, not all of the intended recreational programs are useful, though they do take up leisure time and, viewed as a whole, are probably worth while.
I conclude by suggesting to the hon. member that in general I think his motion has been a waste of time. There are some very serious problems facing the country today,

such as unemployment, with regard to which there have been no new initiatives recently by the government. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) asked today whether any new initiatives were being proposed by the government, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) replied there were none. We are all going home for the summer and are very disappointed at his statement since we were looking forward to talking to our constituents about something. If no new initiatives to combat unemployment are being taken, then the Prime Minister could at least have given us some new alibis to discuss with our constituents.
I see there is only one minister in the House, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), so I should like to ask him directly whether he would write down the names of the three towns of High Level, Fort Chipewyan and Fort Vermillion and ask the cabinet to make a greater effort to ensure that television service is extended to the people in those areas.
To get back to the satellite program, I have had further communication with the CBC and apparently there is a lot more to it than just getting a satellite into the sky. There is also the question of allocating funds and doing preliminary surveys, as well as planning for the construction of receiving stations. While I do not know for sure how long it will take to complete these aspects, I am inclined to think it will be two, three years or more. But if we have to wait another two years before the satellite is put in the sky-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before we adjourn I should like to remind hon. members that tney are invited to join me in Room 16. It will be an occasion to extend greetings and to wish one another pleasant holidays and good luck in any event that may occur in the months ahead.

Evidently, I would ask my hon. colleagues to join me in a moment.

I would also like to add one word. Earlier today hon. members were kind enough to extend warm congratulations to my humble person in the discharge of my work as Speaker. I think at that time I should have acknowledged that any measure of success of the Speaker depends on the co-operation of hon. members. It depends also on the assistance, guidance and counsel of the officials of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On numerous occasions in the past I have had occasion to remind the House, to remind visitors to Parliament and those interested in this institution, of the magnificent contribution made to the House of Commons by our distinguished Clerk, our distinguished Sergeant-at-Arms and the Clerk Assistants who make it possible for us to perform, if I may use the word, and to do our work from day to day as parliamentarians.

On behalf of my colleagues, I want to thank them sincerely and to wish them happy holidays, which they well deserve.

speechtext: You are an outstanding Speaker.
